Big Short's Steve Eisman: "Half of Oracle's Backlog Is Just OpenAI" ©Prathan Chorruangsak from prathan chorruangsak via Canva
Key Takeaways

Oracle stock has lost 54% over the past year, but 80% of the analysts who cover it still rate it a buy.

Steve Eisman says half of Oracle's $638 billion backlog comes from OpenAI. That would make Oracle's growth story largely a bet on one customer's ability to pay.

Oracle's free cash flow was negative $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026, and its total debt rose to $167 billion, so it is borrowing to build that capacity.

OpenAI's $20 billion revenue revision looks like an accounting difference. The thing to watch is whether Oracle's spending starts turning into billed revenue.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) has lost 54% of its value over the past year, yet 80% of the analysts who cover it still rate it a buy, according to CNN's tally.

The bulls are counting the order book. As of its latest quarter, Oracle had $638 billion of signed contracts to supply computing capacity. Its revenue for the year ended May 2026 was $67.4 billion.

Steve Eisman, the investor made famous by The Big Short, looked at that same order book and saw one name. Here's what he said on The Compound and Friends on Oct. 16:

"Oracle is much worse because half of Oracle's backlog is just OpenAI."

Half of $638 billion is about $320 billion, all owed by one private company.

One customer, a lot of building

Eisman led into it with a story from his time at Oppenheimer in the 1990s. A software analyst there refused to help take public a fast-growing company that had only two customers. Her reason: "if one of those customers goes away that's the end of the company."

Oracle has far more than two customers. Eisman's point is that it's more exposed to OpenAI than the bigger cloud providers like Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) are. By his estimate, Anthropic and OpenAI make up 70% of the hyperscalers' AI revenue, and that AI revenue is something like 25% to 30% of their total cloud revenue. At Microsoft and its peers, everything else they sell dilutes that exposure. At Oracle, Eisman puts it at half the backlog.

Wall Street's forecasts lean heavily on that backlog. Consensus has Oracle's revenue almost doubling in two years, from $67.4 billion in fiscal 2026 to $132 billion in fiscal 2028.

Oracle (ORCL): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024–2028 (years to May) (TIKR)

Those 39 analysts are assuming the backlog turns into revenue on schedule. By Eisman's count, OpenAI owns half of it.

The $20 billion that went missing

This is where it gets uncomfortable. Eisman again:

"last week OpenAI came out and said that their annualized revenue at the end of September was 50 billion. A month ago they said 70. What happened to 20? Where'd the 20 go?"

title: Veteran Strategist Warns: Meta Skyrocketed Off-Balance-Sheet Financing by 17X, From “$35 Billion to $600 Billion”

Veteran Strategist Warns: Meta Skyrocketed Off-Balance-Sheet Financing by 17X, From “$35 Billion to $600 Billion”
Roxanna Maglangit
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 10:10 AM CDT 6 min read
META
ORCL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Veteran Strategist Warns: Meta Skyrocketed Off-Balance-Sheet Financing by 17X, From "$35 Billion to $600 Billion" ©Karola G from Pexels and Torsakarin from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Strategist Larry McDonald said on Bloomberg Surveillance that Meta has taken its off-balance-sheet financing from $35 billion to $600 billion to protect its free cash flow.

Meta's own filings back up the size: $279 billion of signed leases that haven't started and $349 billion of non-cancelable commitments as of June 30, 2026, compared with $85.1 billion of reported debt at the end of 2025.

Meta can pay for what it has signed. But those obligations lock in years of AI spending, and its free cash flow fell below $1 billion in the June quarter.

Neocloud bonds and Oracle's cash burn are the early warning signs to watch, and Meta's third-quarter report on Oct. 21 will show whether the commitments kept growing.

Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) owes a lot more than its balance sheet shows. (As usual, the good stuff is in the footnotes.)

On Monday's episode of Bloomberg Surveillance, Larry McDonald, founder of The Bear Traps Report, shared what he'd heard at a Silicon Valley dinner:

"the free cash flow burn of, say, Meta, was so significant a year ago, the projection, that they started, they've taken the off-balance sheet financing from $35 billion to $600 billion"

Why do it? In his words: "It protects their free cash flow."

That's a 17x jump.

Where $600 billion hides

Under US accounting rules, a lease goes on the balance sheet only once it starts. Meta signs data center leases years before the buildings open, and until it moves in, the obligation sits in a footnote. The same is true of its non-cancelable commitments, mostly for third-party cloud capacity, servers and data centers. Those show up on the books only as Meta pays them.

McDonald named the appeal. Meta pays for those buildings as rent over as long as 30 years, which keeps the up-front cost out of its capex line. And with Meta's ad business standing behind the rent, McDonald says banks will happily lend "against their cash flow from Instagram, Facebook, which is juicy."

His numbers hold up in Meta's filings. At the end of March 2025, Meta had about $35 billion of signed leases that hadn't started yet. By June 30, 2026, that figure was $279 billion, on top of $349 billion of non-cancelable commitments: $628 billion in all. (McDonald's starting and ending figures count slightly different things, but the size checks out.) Meta then signed another $68 billion of data center leases in July.

Now compare that with the debt Meta actually reports.

Meta Platforms (META): total debt, $ billions, fiscal 2021–2025 (TIKR)

Reported debt has grown sixfold since 2021, to $85.1 billion at the end of 2025. That's still a fraction of what sits in the footnotes.
